paragraphs.heading: What a rainbow is
paragraphs.text: A rainbow appears when water droplets refract, internally reflect and disperse light, leaving a continuous spectrum in the sky. It takes the shape of a circular arc of many colors. Rain is not the only source: mist, spray and airborne dew can make one too.

paragraphs.heading: Where to look
paragraphs.text: A rainbow made by sunlight always sits in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun. You need drops of water in the air and sunshine coming from behind you at a low angle. That is why rainbows usually show up in the western sky in the morning and the eastern sky in the early evening. The center of the arc always lies on the line running from the Sun to your eye.

paragraphs.heading: Inside a droplet
paragraphs.text: In the main, or primary, rainbow, light bends as it enters a drop, reflects off the back of the drop, and bends again as it leaves. Red ends up on the outer edge of the arc and violet on the inner edge. Each round drop scatters light over a whole circular disc of sky, and red light is spread over a wider angle than blue. Over most of that disc all the colors overlap into white light, so the sky inside the bow looks brighter than outside; at the disc's edge do the colors separate into a rainbow.

paragraphs.heading: Double rainbows
paragraphs.text: In good conditions, a second, larger but fainter arc often shows up about 10° outside the first. Its colors run the other way, with red on its lower side. The best displays come when half the sky is still dark with rain clouds while the sky toward the Sun is clear where you stand. The bright bow then stands out against the dark background.

paragraphs.heading: Full circles and moonbows
paragraphs.text: From the ground a rainbow usually looks like an arc, but from an aeroplane, with enough mist, you can sometimes see a full circle. This can be confused with a glory, though a glory is usually far smaller, covering only 5–20°. On strongly moonlit nights a moonbow can rarely appear. Because people see color poorly in low light, it often looks white.

paragraphs.heading: How many colors
paragraphs.text: The best-known list is Isaac Newton's seven: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, recalled as Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain. Newton first named only five main colors, in 1672, then added orange and indigo to match the number of notes in a musical scale. Today the bow is often split into red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue and violet instead. The way the bands seem distinct is an artefact of human perception. Settling on an exact number of main colors is a somewhat arbitrary choice.

paragraphs.heading: Catching one on camera
paragraphs.text: Fitting the whole half-circle of a rainbow into one photo is hard, because it needs an 84° angle of view. On a 35 mm camera that means a wide-angle lens whose focal length is 19 mm or shorter. Now that software can stitch overlapping photos into a panorama, pictures of the entire arc, and even the second arc, are fairly easy to make.
